summary: Describes RSVP-TE signaling extensions for protecting and restoring just a segment of a GMPLS label switched path. It complements the end-to-end recovery extensions of RFC 4872 and discusses how they interact. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4873 lets a GMPLS network protect or restore one portion of a label-switched path instead of requiring a backup for the whole route. It defines signaling for choosing the portion, building its recovery path, recording that path and reporting failures.

subtitle: RSVP-TE signaling for protecting or restoring only part of a GMPLS path.

tldr.problem: End-to-end recovery needs a protecting path with the same ingress and egress, which may not be available. Existing fast-reroute methods do not cover every recovery type or switching technology described by RFC 4872.
tldr.mechanism: A recovery LSP runs independently from a branch node to a merge node and is associated with the working LSP. SEROs can name these nodes explicitly, or PROTECTION flags can let nodes identify them dynamically.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4873 extends the RFC 4872 recovery types to segments, including overlapping and nested segments, and changes NOTIFY_REQUEST handling. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9270.

today: RFC 4873 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3473 and RFC 4872. It has been updated by RFC 9270.

sections.title: Why Recover a Segment
sections.content:
RFC 4872 defines several forms of GMPLS recovery, but each protects an entire label-switched path (LSP) between the same ingress and egress nodes. A complete protecting path may not be possible even when an alternate route exists around one failed node or link.

RFC 4873 applies the RFC 4872 recovery types to a portion of an LSP. A recovery segment may protect any number of nodes and links, and segments may overlap or be nested. The extensions are intended to work with fast reroute and can be used with it in some cases.

A recovery LSP is signaled independently. Its branch node starts the recovery LSP and its merge node ends it, returning traffic to the protected path.
sections.plainLanguage: A backup route can cover only the part of a network where failures need protection. This RFC defines how to signal that part and connect it back to the original path.

sections.title: Recovery LSPs and Associations
sections.content:
The RFC's example has a working path A-B-C-D-E-F and an alternate path C-G-I-E. The alternate path can protect the spans C-D and D-E and node D, even though an end-to-end protecting LSP from A to F is unavailable.

The branch node initiates the recovery LSP; the merge node terminates it. The recovery LSP uses its own signaling state and identifies the branch and merge in its Sender_Template and Session objects. Intermediate nodes process it using standard signaling procedures. A recovery LSP can itself receive segment or end-to-end protection.

An ASSOCIATION object links a recovery LSP to the LSP it protects. RFC 4873 adds Resource Sharing association type 2 for make-before-break when an LSP endpoint changes. Its association ID must uniquely identify the group, and the RFC says a Resource Sharing association should not be removed once included.
sections.plainLanguage: The branch node starts the alternate path, and the merge node brings it back to the working path. Signaling objects identify which working path the alternate path protects.

sections.title: Explicit Control with SERO
sections.content:
A Secondary Explicit Route Object (SERO) travels in a Path message and can specify where recovery starts and ends. It has the format of an Explicit Route Object and uses object class 200. An SERO should identify the branch node first, then the recovery type in a protection subobject, and the merge node last; route subobjects can specify intermediate hops.

Nodes that are not the named branch pass SEROs onward unchanged. At the branch, the node builds a recovery Path message from the protected LSP's message, assigning a local sender address and new LSP ID, setting the merge node as the endpoint, and building a new explicit route from the SERO. The protection subobject supplies the recovery PROTECTION object, with its R-bit reset.

If recovery setup fails, the branch normally sends a PathErr upstream for the protected LSP with error 21, LSP Segment Protection Failed. When the protected LSP's Required bit is set and recovery state is removed, the error signals removal of the protected path and PathTear is sent downstream on its active branches.
sections.plainLanguage: An upstream node can name the start, end and type of a recovery path. The branch node reads those instructions and creates a separate LSP for the alternate route.

sections.title: Recording Recovery Routes with SRRO
sections.content:
A Secondary Record Route Object (SRRO), class 201, records the route used by a recovery LSP. Transit nodes pass received SRROs onward unchanged. The object can also carry the protection subobject.

In Path messages, a merge node copies the recovery LSP's recorded route into an SRRO on the protected LSP. In Resv messages, the branch node records the recovery route in an SRRO on the protected LSP. Collection is requested with the segment-recording-desired flag in SESSION_ATTRIBUTE, which may be set even when explicit SEROs are not used.

If SRROs make a Resv message too large, subobjects should be removed first. The first two and last subobjects of an SRRO must remain, and the subobject following a removed one must have its L-bit set. If the message remains too large, whole SRROs should be removed.
sections.plainLanguage: SRRO objects carry records of the alternate routes back along the working path. This lets the endpoints see which path each recovery LSP used.

sections.title: Dynamic Control with PROTECTION Flags
sections.content:
Instead of naming branch and merge nodes in a SERO, an upstream node can request dynamic identification using the LSP Segment Recovery Flags in a PROTECTION object. The six-bit Seg.Flags field uses the recovery type values from RFC 4872. The In-Place bit says the requested recovery is already active; the Required bit says failure to establish it should fail the protected LSP.

A transit node with non-zero flags and In-Place clear should decide whether it can provide that recovery type and find a suitable merge node. It must not identify itself dynamically as a branch when a SERO already names it. If it cannot support the request, it processes the Path message normally and leaves the flags unchanged.

A dynamically selected branch builds a recovery LSP and sets In-Place in its PROTECTION object and, while recovery exists, in the original Path message. If dynamic recovery setup fails, the recovery LSP is removed without an error indication upstream; other procedures follow the explicit-control rules.
sections.plainLanguage: An upstream node can request a recovery type without specifying where it starts or ends. Routers that can provide it choose those points; a router that cannot leaves the request unchanged.

sections.title: Security and Notification Changes
sections.content:
The RFC adds signaling objects but no new message types and does not change the relationship between adjacent control-plane routers. SEROs and SRROs reveal more about LSP routes in signaling messages than EROs and RROs alone; the RFC describes this as a very minor risk because the information is already available through routing.

RFC 4873 also changes NOTIFY_REQUEST processing. Branch and merge nodes can add notification requests for recovery and protected LSPs, preserving them as an ordered list. Nodes must propagate later NOTIFY_REQUEST objects in the order received, rather than ignoring them.

The RFC assigns association type 2 for Resource Sharing, object class 200 for SECONDARY_EXPLICIT_ROUTE, class 201 for SECONDARY_RECORD_ROUTE, protection subobject type 37 and error value 21 for LSP Segment Protection Failed.
sections.plainLanguage: Recovery signaling carries extra details about the routes, which can reveal slightly more about network layout. It also lets several notification destinations be carried in order so a node can report a failure to the right place.
